extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (primary) and patent practitioners/attorneys
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining and drafting patent specification and claims with respect to patentability (AIA transition, novelty/obviousness considerations) and the three separate requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (written description, enablement, best mode), including special rules for computer-implemented and means-plus-function claim limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference discloses all claim limitations except a property or function (shift burden)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a prior art reference discloses all limitations of a claim except a property or function and the examiner cannot determine whether the reference inherently possesses the claimed property/function, the examiner may have basis to shift the burden of proof to the applicant (see In re Fitzgerald).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §§ 2112 - 2112.02. Examiner should explain why the burden is shifted and cite supporting authority; include full factual basis on the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference teaches a small genus placing a claimed species in the public possession
rubrics_metrics.description: When a reference discloses a small genus that places a claimed species in the possession of the public, the species may be anticipated or obvious even if genus disclosure would not generally support anticipation under 35 U.S.C. 102.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See In re Schaumann and MPEP §§ 2131.02 and 2144.08. Consider genus/species relationship and whether the species would have been obvious from the genus disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-process: product in reference appears same or obvious variant despite different process
rubrics_metrics.description: When a prior art reference teaches a product that appears to be the same as, or an obvious variant of, the product set forth in a product-by-process claim even if produced by a different process, the product may be anticipated or render the claim obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See In re Marosi, In re Thorpe, and MPEP § 2113. Focus on the product itself, not the process, when assessing anticipation/obviousness of product-by-process claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference discloses all claim limitations except a means-plus-function limitation (equivalence/variant uncertainty)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a reference teaches all claim limitations except a means-plus-function limitation and the examiner is unsure whether the element disclosed in the reference is an equivalent of the claimed element (anticipatory) or whether it is an obvious variant, further analysis is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §§ 2183 - 2184. Determine whether corresponding structure in the specification limits the claimed means-plus-function and whether prior art discloses that structure or an equivalent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlapping claimed and prior-art ranges without specific example within claimed range
rubrics_metrics.description: When the ranges disclosed in the reference and those claimed by the applicant overlap but the reference does not contain a specific example within the claimed range, the overlap may nevertheless support a rejection in appropriate circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See concurring opinion in Ex parte Lee and MPEP § 2131.03. Evaluate whether the overlap and teachings provide a sufficient basis for anticipation or obviousness; explain reasoning on the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: If claim interpretation renders claim(s) indefinite, use 35 U.S.C. 112(b) rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: If, upon claim interpretation, the claims are rendered indefinite, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (definiteness) may be appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how claim language leads to indefiniteness and provide clear reasons on the record linking claim language to 112(b) grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form-paragraph and documentation requirements for making a rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: When using the specified form paragraph for rejections, the examiner must: insert the claim number(s) under rejection, insert appropriate paragraph letter(s), insert the prior art reference relied upon, and provide a full explanation of how the claims could be considered anticipated or obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The form paragraph must be preceded by specified form paragraphs (7.07.aia, 7.08.aia and/or 7.12.aia or form paragraph 7.103) and for some priority situations by form paragraph 7.06. Always provide a full explanation beyond the form paragraph and cite relevant MPEP sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: AIA applicability based on filing date (pre-March 16, 2013)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications filed before March 16, 2013 are governed by pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103; later procedural events such as RCEs or entering national stage do not convert a pre-March 16, 2013 filing into an AIA application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neither filing an RCE nor entry under 35 U.S.C. 371 constitutes filing a new application. See MPEP § 2159.01. Keep record of effective filing dates when determining which statute applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: AIA applies if any claim ever has effective filing date on/after March 16, 2013
rubrics_metrics.description: If an application contains or ever contained at any time a claim having an effective filing date on or after March 16, 2013 (as defined in 35 U.S.C. 100(i)), then AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 apply to the application; a single such claim causes AIA law to apply to the patentability of every claimed invention in the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This applies even if the single AIA-era claim is later canceled. Also applies where an application claims benefit/priority under 120/121/365 to an earlier application that contained such a claim. See MPEP § 2159.02.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments that add AIA-era claims can convert a pre-AIA application to an AIA application
rubrics_metrics.description: If an application filed on or after March 16, 2013 is amended to contain a claim whose effective filing date is on or after March 16, 2013, the application becomes an AIA application — provided the new claim has support under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) in the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The application remains AIA even if the newly added claim is subsequently canceled. Treat any new grounds of rejection necessitated by this change as new grounds for purposes of finality rules (see MPEP § 706.07(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of amendments that introduce new matter (35 U.S.C. 132(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 132(a) prohibits introduction of new matter into the disclosure; if an amendment introduces new matter, the Office follows specific administrative procedures (e.g., new drawings not entered if found to contain new matter; amendments with new matter ordinarily entered but new matter canceled and claims directed to new matter rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §§ 608.02 and 608.04. This process is administrative and for resolving disputes over whether new matter was introduced; maintain clear record and explain rejections for claims presenting new matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant statement required in transition applications (37 CFR 1.55 / 1.78)
rubrics_metrics.description: For nonprovisional applications filed on or after March 16, 2013 that claim benefit/priority to an earlier application filed before March 16, 2013 and that contain or contained at any time a claimed invention having an effective filing date on or after March 16, 2013, the applicant must provide a 37 CFR 1.55 or 1.78 statement to assist the Office in determining applicability of AIA vs pre-AIA statutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant is not required to provide the statement if it was filed in an earlier transition application to which benefit is claimed. See 37 CFR 1.78(c)(6)(i) and MPEP § 2159.04.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must include three separate and distinct requirements under 35 U.S.C. 112(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 112(a) requires (A) a written description of the invention, (B) the manner and process of making and using the invention (enablement), and (C) the best mode contemplated by the inventor for carrying out the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three elements are separate statutory requirements (applicable to applications filed on or after Sept. 16, 2012); analogous requirements exist in pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph. Cite statutory language and MPEP § 2161 heading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description requirement is separate and distinct from enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: Written description and enablement are distinct inquiries: written description shows the inventor possessed the claimed invention at filing, while enablement shows how to make and use the invention without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Ariad (en banc), Vas-Cath, Barker, and related cases. Examiners must assess written description and enablement independently and explain deficiencies separately on the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description: must convey possession of claimed subject matter (genus/species, breadth considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: To satisfy written description, the specification must describe the claimed invention in sufficient detail that a person of ordinary skill in the art would reasonably conclude the inventor had possession of the claimed invention at filing. The sufficiency varies with the nature/scope of claims; genus claims require adequate species support depending on state of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Ariad, Hynix, LizardTech, Rivera and related cases. Consider whether generic/functional claim language is supported by the disclosure; generic statements alone may be insufficient. Provide factual explanation tying disclosure to claimed scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-implemented functional claim limitations: written description must disclose computer, steps/algorithm, and/or corresponding structure
rubrics_metrics.description: For computer-implemented functional claim limitations, the specification must disclose the computer and the necessary steps and/or algorithm (or other sufficient structure) that perform the claimed function so one skilled in the art can conclude inventor possessed the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algorithm can be expressed as math formula, prose, flowchart, or other understandable terms. Simply restating the function is not necessarily sufficient. See Vasudevan Software, Finisar, Microsoft Computer Dictionary, and MPEP §§ 2163 - 2163.07(b), 2181 subsection IV. If insufficient, make 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or 112 first paragraph rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function limitations require disclosure of corresponding structure/materials/acts (112(f) / sixth paragraph)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (means or step plus function), the specification must disclose sufficient corresponding structure, materials, or acts to perform the entire claimed function. Failure to provide sufficient corresponding structure can also implicate 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (indefiniteness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If corresponding structure is missing or insufficient, make a written description rejection under 112(a) and a 112(b) rejection for failure to particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention. See In re Donaldson and MPEP § 2181.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode requirement: subjective knowledge and objective disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Best mode requires two inquiries: (1) subjective — whether the inventor actually knew of a best mode of practicing the invention at filing; (2) objective — whether that best mode was disclosed in sufficient detail to allow one skilled in the art to practice it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of concealment (accidental or intentional) is relevant to best mode. For software best mode, disclosure of functions is normally sufficient because writing code is within skill of the art; flowcharts/source code are not generally required. See In re Gay, Fonar, and related MPEP §§ 2165 - 2165.04.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement: must enable full scope of claimed invention without undue experimentation (Wands factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Enablement requires that the specification teach those skilled in the art how to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention without undue experimentation. The In re Wands factors guide assessment: (1) claim breadth, (2) nature of the invention, (3) state of prior art, (4) level of skill, (5) predictability in the art, (6) amount of direction provided by inventor, (7) existence of working examples, (8) quantity of experimentation needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh all Wands factors; do not treat enablement as single-fact determination. Cite In re Wands and MPEP §§ 2164 - 2164.08(c). If examiner has reasonable basis to question enablement, place burden on applicant to rebut with factual demonstration (In re Brown, In re Scarbrough, In re Doyle).

rubrics_metrics.name: When claim language is functional but does not invoke 112(f), broad claim scope raises enablement concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim recites the ability to perform a function without invoking 112(f) and does not limit to particular structure, it is typically construed broadly to cover any embodiments that perform the function; this broad scope raises concern whether the specification enables the full scope of the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether disclosure enables all embodiments covered by the broad functional language. Applicants choosing broad functional claim language risk invalidity for lack of enablement. Cite In re Swinehart, AK Steel, In re Moore.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner must establish reasonable basis for enablement rejections; applicant must rebut with evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Before sustaining an enablement rejection, USPTO personnel must establish on the record a reasonable basis for questioning adequacy of disclosure to enable one of ordinary skill to make and use the claimed invention without undue experimentation. After that, the applicant has the opportunity to rebut with factual evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Brown, In re Ghiron, In re Doyle, In re Scarbrough and MPEP guidance. Provide clear factual reasoning supporting the examiner's position and identify specific deficiencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims scope must be commensurate with enablement (claims no broader than enabled scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of patent claims must be less than or equal to the scope of enablement provided by the specification; claims broader than enabled disclosure may be invalid for lack of enablement or written description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Sitrick, MagSil examples where overly broad claims were invalidated because specification could not enable the full claimed scope. Explain how claimed elements exceed disclosure and why undue experimentation would be required.
